reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: A benign sensory parasomnia in which the patient perceives a sudden, loud imagined noise or a sense of explosion in the head during transitions into or out of sleep
The sound may resemble a bang, clash, gunshot or electrical discharge and can be accompanied by a perceived flash of light
There is a startle or sense of fright but typically little or no pain, which distinguishes it from headache disorders
Episodes are brief and cause abrupt arousal, sometimes with palpitations or a feeling of fear
It becomes more common with age and with sleep deprivation or stress
Reassurance about the harmless nature of the phenomenon is the mainstay of management
Diagnosis is clinical, but recurrent or atypical events may warrant exclusion of nocturnal seizures or other causes
reference.pathophysiology: Exploding head syndrome is thought to arise from a transient disturbance in the normal shutting-down of brainstem and reticular activity during the wake-to-sleep transition. Rather than a smooth switch, a brief burst of neuronal activity, possibly within auditory pathways, is proposed to generate the perception of a sudden loud sound. It is regarded as a benign phenomenon of the sleep-wake boundary rather than evidence of structural disease.
additionalDifferentials: Nocturnal seizures, especially of temporal lobe origin
Auditory hallucinations of a psychiatric disorder
additionalInvestigations: Clinical history distinguishing a painless sensory event from headache
Sleep and symptom diary noting the timing relative to sleep onset or waking
Polysomnography if the diagnosis is unclear or seizures are suspected
Neuroimaging only when atypical features or red flags are present
Review of sleep hygiene, stress and sleep deprivation
redFlags: Significant pain accompanying the event, suggesting a headache disorder rather than exploding head syndrome
Stereotyped events with other features suggesting nocturnal seizures
Progressive change in the frequency or character of episodes
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often self-limiting; episodes tend to wax and wane, and many patients improve simply with reassurance and attention to sleep and stress, without needing medication.
pitfalls: Mistaking the event for a serious headache such as thunderclap headache
Overlooking nocturnal seizures when events are stereotyped
Causing unnecessary anxiety by over-investigating a benign phenomenon
Neglecting contributory sleep deprivation and stress
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Reassurance and education about the benign, self-limiting nature of the phenomenon as the mainstay of management
Optimise sleep hygiene and correct sleep deprivation, which reduces episode frequency
Address contributing stress and anxiety with relaxation techniques or cognitive behavioural therapy
Reserve pharmacotherapy such as tricyclic antidepressants (clomipramine, amitriptyline) for frequent, distressing episodes
Perform polysomnography if the diagnosis is uncertain or nocturnal seizures are suspected
Provide follow-up, as episodes typically wax and wane and often settle with reassurance alone
